lesson.title: Talking to Python One Line at a Time: The REPL
lesson.summary: The Python REPL is an interactive session where you type one statement at a time and immediately see its result, making it a fast way to experiment with the same interpreter you learned about in the previous chapter.
lesson.body:
REPL stands for Read, Eval, Print, Loop, and it describes exactly what happens when you start Python without giving it a file to run. If you type python at a terminal with no filename after it, the interpreter starts an interactive session and shows a prompt, usually three greater-than signs, >>>, waiting for you to type something. From there, the interpreter reads whatever single statement or expression you typed, evaluates it using the same underlying interpreter machinery described in the previous chapter, prints the resulting value automatically if there is one, and then loops back to wait for your next input. This cycle, read, evaluate, print, loop, repeats for as long as the session stays open.

The REPL's automatic printing behavior is its most distinctive feature, and it is worth tracing carefully because it surprises many beginners. Consider a session that looks like this:

>>> 2 + 2
4
>>> x = 10
>>> x * 3
30
>>> print("hi")
hi

The first line, 2 + 2, is an expression, meaning it produces a value, and the REPL automatically displays that value, 4, without you needing to call print. The second line, x = 10, is an assignment statement rather than an expression with a value to show, so the REPL displays nothing at all, it simply performs the assignment and returns to the prompt. The third line, x * 3, is an expression again, so its value, 30, is displayed automatically. The fourth line explicitly calls print("hi"), which prints hi as its side effect. The print function itself technically returns a special value called None once it finishes, but the REPL is written to suppress displaying None, so you only see the output hi and not an extra None printed afterward.

This is quite different from running a saved script, where nothing is displayed automatically no matter what kind of statement or expression appears on a line, because a script simply runs from top to bottom and only print calls produce visible output. The REPL's auto-display is a convenience built specifically for interactive use, and it only works because the REPL evaluates one statement at a time and immediately has a value ready to show, rather than running a whole file's worth of statements before anything happens.

The REPL is valuable because it shortens the feedback loop between having an idea and seeing whether it works. Instead of writing a whole file, saving it, and running it just to check what a single expression does, you can type that one expression directly and see the answer in under a second. Professional programmers use the REPL constantly to test how a function behaves, check what a piece of syntax does, or explore an unfamiliar library one small step at a time, before committing that logic into a larger saved program.

It is worth noting what the REPL is not good at. Because each session is temporary and disappears once you close the terminal window, the REPL is a poor place to build anything you intend to keep, reuse, or share with someone else, since retyping dozens of lines from scratch every time is impractical and error-prone. The REPL also has no simple way to save its history as a runnable program by itself. For any piece of logic worth keeping around, the natural next step is to move it out of the interactive session and into a saved file. That larger, saved kind of program is exactly what the next chapter covers.
